methodology.date: Exact visit date remains null unless verified. An assigned year is approximate, and a range is retained as a range.

methodology.musicAndDining: Attending a restaurant with live jazz does not automatically count as a distinct concert. Require a separately confirmed performance before adding a concert record.
methodology.awardFocusedCollection: Default Culture Passport Dining chapter shows only venues with verified historical Michelin inclusion or James Beard recognition of restaurant itself or chef at that restaurant. methodology.curated: Default Culture Passport dining views show confirmed restaurants with documented Michelin Guide recognition (star, Bib, Selected, historic Plate) or directly associated James Beard awards, finalists or semifinalists. Those awards retain their recipient and year. Chef awards at unrelated restaurants or historical awards dated after a dinner may be context, not proof of qualification at the meal date. Unverified and outside-scope visits stay in archive but are hidden from curated browsing by default.
methodology.featuredExceptions: Venue-specific Michelin/JBF honors are the default inclusion criteria, but the user's express favorites Sauvage, Gunther & Co., Death & Co Denver and provisional favorite The Majestic are displayed in the primary collection despite no established qualifying award. FiNO was added as a user-selected confirmed 2026 visit without award recognition; this does not imply it is a personal favorite.
methodology.beverages: Stand-alone cocktail bars are type=bar, never counted as restaurants. James Beard Outstanding Bar Program includes bar semifinalists. Never borrow recognition from another location within a chain.
methodology.repeatVisits: A venue may be visited in multiple years. Each confirmed year is represented as a separate experience record with a stable unique ID, sharing one venue ID; do not manufacture precise calendar dates or collapse years into one event.
methodology.reservationEvidence: Date and party size from completed reservation screenshots are documentary evidence, not independent proof of check-in or dining. Only directly restaurant-level Michelin/JBF recognition enters the curated collection automatically. The user explicitly excluded Le Fou Frog: it must not enter any deployed venue/experience ledger, even though its date appears in private conversation uploads.
methodology.storyFirst: Each published entry leads with a grounded personal memory, atmosphere, or occasion. Dates are retained in provenance but the public timeline emphasizes approximate years, seasons, and meaningful events. Never fabricate meals, companion details, specific actions, or feelings not supplied by the user.
methodology.dateDisplay: Date/party details are backend evidence, available in a collapsed archive-notes section on experience pages, not default cards or timeline. Exact date may be shown only if necessary to a user-given occasion (Valentine's Day, etc.).
methodology.familyStory: A venue may carry a narrative across sister restaurants or expansions. Guide badges identify the recognized original without treating each branch as a separate unverified award.
methodology.criterionAudit: Keep separate: verified Michelin Guide inclusion (stars, Bib, Selected/historical Plate), James Beard semifinalist/finalist/winner at the specific venue or chef while working there, explicitly featured personal memories, user-confirmed history without award, uncertain leads, and reservation-only evidence. Never count unverified founders' awards from unrelated restaurants or award years as the historical dining year.
methodology.stageMemories: Confirmed live outings can be recorded with a provisional production title. Verify the tour period and venue independently but do not infer exact performance dates; labels are about the memory.
methodology.culturalExperiences: Concert, festival, theatrical, live television, magic and opera entries can be supported by user recollections or personal event archive screenshots without Michelin/James Beard recognition. Show exact performance dates only when supported; a run's date window never proves a particular night.
methodology.reservationDisambiguation: Confirmed venue attendance never makes a completed reservation date a confirmed meal date. A booking without direct visit confirmation is reservation_only and excluded from published experiences. Store booking date, party size, and provenance under reservations, not visit.date.
methodology.confirmedVisitPublicInclusion: Every direct user-confirmed visit is included in the visitor-data candidate collection without an external-award gate. Brewery-brand visits count as confirmed experiences even if a precise taproom, city or date is unknown; these remain unmapped until a legitimate location cue is available. Public release of story wording requires separate editorial review; this inclusion instruction does not automatically approve every story or launch the site.

Their restaurant's hospitality and setting provide a richer backdrop for the Valentine's Day memory.

story.headline: Steaks and jazz inside a century of Kansas City history
paragraphs: Before the name came back, you remembered the combination: a wonderful Kansas City steakhouse with a jazz room down in the basement. That distinctive atmosphere brought you back to The Majestic. The year of your dinner remains open; the place itself is confirmed.

The building at 931 Broadway was originally Fitzpatrick's Saloon, opened in 1911. Its cellar took on a different life during Prohibition, when the lower level was used as a speakeasy. That room is today's Jazz Club—a link between the city's storied nightlife and the steakhouse you remembered.

The historic building was restored in the 1980s, and the Majestic name returned to the site in the early 1990s. The current restaurant opened under that name in November 2009, bringing dry-aged Kansas City steaks and live jazz together. It is an experience worth keeping for its atmosphere, regardless of Michelin or James Beard status.

story.headline: A basement cocktail room that helped change Kansas City
paragraphs: You remembered Manifesto as an amazing cocktail-bar experience. What stands out is its hidden, subterranean character—a room defined by candlelight, old stone walls, and carefully made drinks. The exact night is unknown, and there's no need to invent one.

Bartender Ryan Maybee opened Manifesto in 2009 beneath the building at 1924 Main Street. story.headline: A quiet table in Lincoln Park, after marathon week
paragraphs: The memorable part begins before reaching the table. North Pond sits not on a busy downtown restaurant row, but tucked into the trees beside a pond in Lincoln Park. Its low Arts and Crafts-style building was constructed in 1912 as a warming shelter for ice skaters; decades later, that same refuge became a place for thoughtful, seasonal American cooking.

The restaurant's reputation was built in no small part by chef Bruce Sherman, whose focus on Midwestern ingredients earned him the James Beard Foundation's Best Chef: Great Lakes award in 2012. Sherman stepped away from daily kitchen leadership at the end of 2019, but the restaurant's identity endured.

In October 2021, during the week after the Chicago Marathon, this was one of the restaurants worth seeking out. That year's Michelin Guide had awarded North Pond one star months before the meal. The precise evening and dishes are not recorded; what survives is the setting, the post-race trip to Chicago, and a restaurant whose story reaches back more than a century.

story.headline: A library below the city
paragraphs: The clue was brief: 'The Library in Gilt Bar.' A friend's message put this tucked-away Chicago space back into the collection. The personal occasion and year are still uncertain; the name itself is the piece worth preserving.

The Library is a basement room reached through a discreet door beneath Gilt Bar in River North. Wine-colored walls, leather and velvet seating, old books and low-hanging chandeliers give it the feel of a private Prohibition-era hideaway. It is part of Gilt Bar, not a separate restaurant elsewhere in town.

Michelin includes Gilt Bar in its Chicago Bib Gourmand selection. That honor belongs to the restaurant above and around the Library, not to an independently awarded basement cocktail bar. For this archive, the real reason to keep the entry is the atmosphere—and a name recovered through a friend's memory.

story.headline: From pre-Prohibition whiskey to a renewed Electric Park
paragraphs: J. Rieger & Co. began in Kansas City in 1887, when Jacob Rieger developed a nationally successful mail-order whiskey business. Prohibition ended its first era. Andy Rieger and Kansas City bartender Ryan Maybee revived the brand in 2014, bringing a historic name into the city's modern cocktail culture.

In 2019, the business opened its new home in the restored Heim Brewery bottling plant at 2700 Guinotte Avenue, a 1901 industrial building in the East Bottoms. The preservation project reconnected Kansas City distilling, architecture, and neighborhood history. Missouri Preservation gave J. Rieger & Co. a 2020 Preserve Missouri Award.

That setting became more than a distillery visit: I have been to five distinct experiences here. Electric Park Garden Bar transformed a former loading-dock area into an architectural award-winning urban garden. The Hey! Hey! Club made a separate name for itself in the cocktail world. Monogram Lounge overlooks the working production floor; the separately identified Tasting Room features a marble bar and connects to a glass-enclosed Atrium. Sippin' Santa is the immersive holiday tiki pop-up that has appeared in different on-site spaces in different years. A visit to the Tasting Room does not, by itself, confirm a guided distillery tour or a particular spirits tasting.

My own visits are confirmed; the year of each outing, what I drank, and who joined me are not recorded. The honors below are precise: design awards belong to Electric Park, a preservation award belongs to the wider restored site, and the 2020 regional cocktail-bar honor belongs to the Hey! Hey! Club. The Monogram whiskey label's accolades are not awards to the Monogram Lounge.

story.headline: The night UMBC made history—and a first dinner at Salt
paragraphs: March 16, 2018 is the date tied to my first visit to Salt: A New American Tavern on East Pratt Street in Baltimore. It's easy to remember because that was the night UMBC shocked the top-seeded University of Virginia in the NCAA men's basketball tournament.

UMBC's 74–54 victory in Charlotte was the first time a No. 16 seed defeated a No. 1 seed in the men's tournament. That sporting moment fixes this restaurant memory to a particular night; it doesn't establish that I attended the basketball game or watched it from Salt.

Salt was a Butchers Hill New American tavern known for duck-fat fries, its foie-gras burger, and an exposed-brick dining room. It had received a 2006 Baltimore Magazine Best of Baltimore honor for burger and fries. Those are restaurant history, not a claim about the dishes ordered on my visit.

Salt's regular dinner service ended on August 11, 2018, just five months after the visit. The space later reopened as Marta, a separate restaurant. I want the original Salt experience preserved in my Culture Passport even though no Michelin or James Beard award for Salt has been established.
